newsitem.title: USA: Intel profits jump 40 percent in quarter.
newsitem.headline: Intel profits jump 40 percent in quarter.

text.p: Intel Corp., powered by strong sales of its Pentium and Pentium Pro processors, reported a 40 percent jump in third quarter profits Monday, surpassing even the most optimistic Wall Street estimates.
The world's largest chip maker earned $1.3 billion in the quarter ended in September, up from $931 million in the 1995 quarter. Revenues rose 23 percent to $5.14 billion.

The profits, which equalled $1.48 a share, easily surpassed Wall Street's consensus estimate of $1.25, sending Intel's shares sharply higher in after-hours trading. In the year-ago quarter, Intel earned $1.05 a share, including an a one-time gain of 3 cents a share.

"Phenomenal quarter," said analyst Mark Edelstone of Prudential Securities. "It points out two things" -- the strength of sales of personal computers, where Intel's chips are a mainstay, and Intel's solid manufacturing, he added.
Intel reported its gross margins jumped to 57.2 percent from 53.5 percent in the second quarter, helped largely by a better product mix.
As the supplier of the microprocessors used in the vast majority of personal computers, Intel is often regarded as a bellwether of PC industry fortunes.
Traders said Intel rose $6.875 to $114.50 after hours. It had closed during the day at $107.625 on Nasdaq.

"We are delighted with the excellent acceptance of Pentium and Pentium Pro processor-based PCs and servers, which has produced a stronger third quarter than we had originally expected," Intel President Andrew Grove said in a statement.
So strong were microprocessor sales that many of Intel's manufacturing plants were running at 100 percent capacity, chief financial officer Andy Bryant said in a conference call.
Last month, Intel surprised analysts by predicting third quarter revenues would be about 5 percent above the second quarter, compared with an earlier forecast of flat sales.
That outlook, however, proved to be conservative as third quarter revenues jumped 11 percent from the second quarter.
Intel said the third quarter reflected the strong acceptance of its Pentium and Pentium Pro microprocessors -- the powerful chips that are the brains of some 85 percent of new personal computers.

Bryant said Pentium and Pentium Pro sales provided the jump in revenues for Intel. In fact sales of other products, such as flash memory chips and motherboards, were slightly down in unit volume from the second quarter or flat.
Intel's decision to postpone price cuts on its mainstream Pentium microprocessors this quarter also boosted revenues.
Intel also said it had record orders in the quarter, and that orders booked even exceeded sales shipped.

Intel, which normally provides a detailed outlook for the coming quarter, refrained from making any foward-looking statements, citing concerns about the possible adoption, and effect, of a proposed California ballot initiative.
Intel said the initiative, called Proposition 211, could "significantly increase the exposure to frivolous stockholder lawsuits for all companies with a California presence."

"Although passage of this measure is uncertain, Intel does not intend to assume the risk of making forward-looking statements concerning the company's business outlook," the company said. "Accordingly, Intel will not include such statements in the company's communications with stockholders and the financial community except as required by law."
Intel said it would review its policy after the initiative is voted on Nov. 5.

Sales for the first nine months of 1996 rose 24 percent to $14.41 billion from $11.62 billion a year ago, and net income grew 20 percent to $3.25 billion from $2.70 billion. Earnings per share grew to $3.67 from $3.06.
